source.title: High-dimensional ridge regression with random features for non-identically distributed data with a variance profile

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly sweeps random-feature width and measures predictive risk for double-descent behavior, but studies random-feature ridge regression with variance profiles rather than the original deep-network setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports predictive-risk outcomes for width sweeps. Risk-approximation comparisons are not recorded as separate rows because they assess the approximations, not a distinct double-descent condition. Cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper sweeps random-feature width m in RF ridge regression on non-iid variance-profile data and reports predictive-risk peaks. Belkin et al. already used random features, so this is a new data setting (heteroscedastic mixture designs) for a known model class, not a new method.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The main conclusion is that the derived asymptotic equivalents for training and test risk are sharp for non-iid variance-profile data. A secondary point is that these models show double descent for small λ, with peak location (m = n vs m = p) governed by activation nonlinearity, as previously reported for iid data.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random-feature ridge regression with a fixed random first layer, row-dependent diagonal variance profiles, and predictive-risk measurements; it does not reproduce the original deep-network setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak location changes with activation nonlinearity: near-linear activations are associated with m = p, while more nonlinear activations are associated with m = n. For the reported x³ experiments, the peak sharpens as λ decreases.

fits_no_version.finding: For data with a variance profile, the location of the risk peak (m = n or m = p) depends on the degree of nonlinearity of the activation function.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In random-feature regression, the peak sits at m = p for near-linear activations and at m = n for strongly nonlinear ones.

record.problems: The experiments use simulated predictors rather than raw MNIST images, and the numerical peak results are described qualitatively without reported uncertainty. The paper's theoretical analysis assumes odd polynomial activations, although some experiments also show non-polynomial activations.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; the RF first layer is fixed.
No sweep over sample size n at fixed m.
Model classes other than RF ridge regression; quantitative depth of the second descent.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested. The authors only remark that near-linearity shapes effective complexity, moving the peak to m = p.
Label noise is not varied, optimally tuned λ is not tested, and no multiple peaks appear within a single curve.
No re-counting of parameters by an effective measure.

missing.what: Figure 4 curve for tanh(cx) with c = 1 (intermediate nonlinearity), giving the peak location between the two regimes

record.verdict_notes: All double-descent evidence is qualitative, read from figure descriptions with no numeric risks or uncertainty. The paper's main contribution is theoretical (risk equivalents); the double-descent observations are illustrative. The m = p peak is attributed to prior work [15] (d'Ascoli et al.) and reproduced here in a new setting.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random features with a fixed first layer, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sweep over training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
The tested class is random-feature ridge regression; other model classes are not tested.

The paper discusses peak locations changing with activation nonlinearity, but does not test whether a single measure of effective complexity predicts the location across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.
The paper varies ridge regularization and reports how the peak changes. It does not vary label noise, test optimal tuning, or report triple or multiple descent.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure or test of whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.
